question: A tenant restaurant owner installs a large walk-in cooler that is bolted to the floor for use in her business. Under the law of fixtures, this item is best classified as a:
choice_a: Trade fixture, which the tenant may remove before the lease ends as long as she repairs any damage
choice_b: Real property fixture that automatically transfers to the landlord regardless of the lease terms
choice_c: Emblement that must be harvested before the lease terminates
choice_d: License that expires automatically when the tenancy ends
explanation: Trade fixtures are items a business tenant installs to conduct its trade; even though attached, they remain the tenant's personal property and may be removed before the lease expires, provided the tenant repairs any resulting damage to the premises.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A farmer leases land and plants a crop of wheat during the growing season. The lease expires before the wheat is harvested. Under the doctrine of emblements, the crop is treated as:
choice_a: Real property that transfers automatically to the landlord at the end of the lease
choice_b: Personal property (a chattel) that the tenant farmer is entitled to harvest even after the lease ends
choice_c: A fixture that must remain attached to the land permanently
choice_d: Common property owned jointly by landlord and tenant
explanation: Emblements are annual, cultivated crops produced by a tenant's labor. They are treated as personal property, and the doctrine allows the tenant farmer the right to re-enter and harvest the crop even after the tenancy has ended.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A seller removes an ordinary above-ground dishwasher that simply plugs into an outlet and is not built into the cabinetry, taking it with her when she moves. A buyer objects that it should have stayed. Under general fixture law, who is correct?
choice_a: The buyer, because all kitchen appliances are legally fixtures regardless of attachment
choice_b: The seller, because anything purchased more than five years ago is automatically personal property
choice_c: The seller, because a freestanding appliance that is not physically attached to the structure is presumed to be personal property
choice_d: The buyer, because the item was listed in the multiple listing service description of the kitchen
explanation: Method of attachment is a core fixture test. An appliance that is merely plugged in and not bolted, wired in, or built into the structure is ordinarily personal property, so the seller may remove it unless the contract specifically includes it.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: An appraiser is asked to determine whether a custom greenhouse attached to a home passed with the sale. Which of the following fixture tests asks whether removing the item would cause significant damage to the real property?
choice_a: The adaptability of the item to the property's use
choice_b: The intention of the party who installed the item
choice_c: The relationship between the parties to the transaction
choice_d: The method and permanence of attachment
explanation: The method-and-permanence-of-attachment test looks at how firmly and permanently an item is affixed, including whether removal would cause substantial damage to the structure -- a strong indicator the item has become a fixture.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A legal description begins 'Beginning at the iron pipe at the northeast corner of Lot 4, thence South 200 feet, thence West 150 feet, thence North 200 feet, thence East 150 feet to the point of beginning.' This is an example of a:
choice_a: Metes and bounds description
choice_b: Lot and block description
choice_c: Government (rectangular) survey description
choice_d: Street address description
explanation: Metes and bounds descriptions identify a parcel using a point of beginning, then a series of courses (directions) and distances that trace the boundary back to that same starting point, which is exactly the pattern shown here.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A deed describes property as 'Lot 12, Block 3, Meadowbrook Estates, as recorded in Plat Book 22, Page 14, of the county land records.' This method of legal description relies primarily on:
choice_a: A system of principal meridians and base lines dividing land into 6-mile-square townships
choice_b: A recorded subdivision plat map that has already been surveyed and filed with the county
choice_c: A point of beginning followed by compass directions and distances
choice_d: The property's assessed value for tax purposes
explanation: Lot and block descriptions reference a specific lot and block number shown on a recorded subdivision plat map, which itself contains the detailed metes-and-bounds or survey data for the entire subdivision.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: Under the government (rectangular) survey system, a township is a square area measuring:
choice_a: 1 mile by 1 mile, containing 640 acres
choice_b: 36 miles by 36 miles, containing 6 sections
choice_c: 6 miles by 6 miles, containing 36 sections
choice_d: 1 mile by 1 mile, containing 36 sections
explanation: In the government survey system, a township is a 6-mile-by-6-mile square (36 square miles), which is subdivided into 36 sections, each one mile square.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: Under the government (rectangular) survey system, one full section of land contains how many acres?
choice_a: 36 acres
choice_b: 160 acres
choice_c: 6 acres
choice_d: 640 acres
explanation: A section is one square mile, and one square mile equals 640 acres. Sections are commonly divided further into halves, quarters, and quarter-quarters for smaller parcels.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: When an appraiser calculates a single-family home's gross living area (GLA), which of the following is typically EXCLUDED?
choice_a: An unfinished basement and an attached garage
choice_b: A finished, heated second-floor bedroom
choice_c: A finished, heated first-floor family room
choice_d: A finished, heated sunroom that is part of the main structure and heated by the same system
explanation: Gross living area generally includes only finished, heated, above-grade living space. Unfinished basements and garages, even if attached, are excluded from GLA and reported separately.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: In commercial office leasing, the difference between rentable square footage and usable square footage is generally accounted for by:
choice_a: The square footage of the tenant's private storage unit in the basement
choice_b: A load factor (or common area factor) representing the tenant's proportionate share of shared spaces such as lobbies, hallways, and restrooms
choice_c: The total square footage of the entire building regardless of tenant
choice_d: The parking area assigned exclusively to that tenant
explanation: Usable square footage is the space a tenant physically occupies; rentable square footage adds a load factor reflecting the tenant's pro-rata share of common areas like lobbies and corridors, and rent is typically charged on the rentable figure.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A rectangular showroom measures 40 feet by 60 feet. What is its total square footage?
choice_a: 2,000 square feet
choice_b: 1,800 square feet
choice_c: 2,400 square feet
choice_d: 3,000 square feet
explanation: Area of a rectangle equals length multiplied by width: 40 feet x 60 feet = 2,400 square feet.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A parcel of land measures 435.6 feet by 1,000 feet. Approximately how many acres is this?
choice_a: 1 acre
choice_b: 100 acres
choice_c: 43.56 acres
choice_d: 10 acres
explanation: One acre equals 43,560 square feet. The parcel's area is 435.6 x 1,000 = 435,600 square feet, and 435,600 divided by 43,560 equals 10 acres.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A property borders a slow-moving, non-navigable river. The water rights that attach to this property because of its location along the river are known as:
choice_a: Riparian rights
choice_b: Littoral rights
choice_c: Prior appropriation rights
choice_d: Avulsion rights
explanation: Riparian rights belong to owners of land bordering flowing waters such as rivers and streams. On non-navigable waterways, the riparian owner's title typically extends to the center (thread) of the waterway.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A property is located on the shore of a large lake. The rights this owner holds regarding the lake's water and shoreline are known as:
choice_a: Riparian rights
choice_b: Littoral rights
choice_c: Subsurface rights
choice_d: Police power rights
explanation: Littoral rights apply to property bordering large, substantially non-flowing bodies of water such as lakes, seas, and oceans. Littoral owners generally hold title to the mean high-water mark, with the land below belonging to the public or the state.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: In several western states, water rights in rivers and streams are allocated not based on adjacent land ownership but on which of the following doctrines?
choice_a: Riparian doctrine, under which only adjacent landowners may use the water at all
choice_b: Littoral doctrine, which governs only ocean and lake frontage
choice_c: Prior appropriation, under which the first person to put the water to beneficial use has the superior right
choice_d: Escheat doctrine, under which unclaimed water rights revert to the state
explanation: The prior appropriation doctrine, used in many western states, grants water rights based on who first put the water to beneficial use and when, regardless of whether that user's land actually touches the water source.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A landowner sells the coal and natural gas beneath her property to a mining company while retaining ownership of the surface. This is an example of:
choice_a: An easement in gross benefiting the mining company
choice_b: A license that automatically expires after one year
choice_c: Escheat of the mineral estate to the state
choice_d: Severance of mineral rights from surface rights, creating a subsurface estate separate from the surface estate
explanation: Mineral rights can be severed (separated) from surface rights and conveyed independently, creating two distinct estates in the same land -- a subsurface mineral estate and a surface estate -- that can be owned by different parties.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A developer purchases the right to construct a building in the empty space above an existing rail terminal without owning the land or the terminal itself. What has the developer acquired?
choice_a: Air rights
choice_b: Riparian rights
choice_c: A leasehold estate in the terminal
choice_d: Subsurface rights
explanation: Air rights are the rights to use, control, or occupy the vertical space above a parcel of land. They can be sold or leased separately from the surface, commonly seen with construction over rail yards or highways in dense urban areas.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A bank records a mortgage against a homeowner's property to secure repayment of a loan. This mortgage is best classified as what type of encumbrance?
choice_a: An easement appurtenant
choice_b: A financial lien against the property
choice_c: A deed restriction
choice_d: An encroachment
explanation: A lien is a financial encumbrance that gives a creditor a claim against property as security for a debt. A mortgage is a voluntary lien the owner places on the property to secure the loan used to purchase or refinance it.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: Parcel A has no direct access to a public road except by crossing Parcel B. A recorded easement allows the owner of Parcel A to cross Parcel B for ingress and egress, and this right transfers automatically to future owners of Parcel A. This is an example of:
choice_a: An easement in gross, personal to the current owner of Parcel A only
choice_b: A license, which is revocable at any time
choice_c: An easement appurtenant, with Parcel A as the dominant estate and Parcel B as the servient estate
choice_d: An encroachment onto Parcel B
explanation: An easement appurtenant benefits one parcel (the dominant estate) and burdens another (the servient estate), and it runs with the land, automatically passing to successive owners of both parcels.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A utility company holds a recorded right to maintain power lines across a homeowner's land, but this right is not tied to ownership of any neighboring parcel and belongs to the utility company itself. This is an example of:
choice_a: An easement appurtenant
choice_b: A license
choice_c: A deed restriction
choice_d: An easement in gross
explanation: An easement in gross benefits a specific person or company rather than a neighboring parcel of land. Utility easements are the classic example, since there is no dominant estate -- only a servient estate burdened for the utility's benefit.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A homeowner gives a neighbor verbal permission to walk across her backyard as a shortcut to the lake. The homeowner can revoke this permission at any time. This arrangement is best described as a:
choice_a: License
choice_b: Easement appurtenant
choice_c: Easement by necessity
choice_d: Deed restriction
explanation: A license is a personal, revocable, and non-assignable permission to use another's land for a specific purpose. Unlike an easement, it does not run with the land and can be withdrawn by the landowner at will.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A survey reveals that a neighbor's fence extends 3 feet onto the subject property along the shared boundary line. This physical intrusion is called an:
choice_a: Easement by prescription
choice_b: Encroachment
choice_c: Riparian right
choice_d: Emblement
explanation: An encroachment occurs when a structure or improvement, such as a fence, wall, or roof overhang, unlawfully extends onto an adjoining owner's property, typically discovered through a boundary survey.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: Three unrelated investors purchase an office building together. Their deed grants them unequal ownership percentages (50%, 30%, and 20%), and each may sell, transfer, or will his or her share independently without the consent of the others. Upon the death of one investor, that share passes to his heirs rather than to the surviving co-owners. This is a:
choice_a: Joint tenancy with right of survivorship
choice_b: Tenancy by the entirety
choice_c: Tenancy in common
choice_d: Community property
explanation: Tenancy in common allows co-owners to hold unequal, undivided interests, each freely transferable and inheritable, with no right of survivorship -- exactly the arrangement described.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: Two unrelated business partners take title to a warehouse as joint tenants with right of survivorship. When one partner dies, what happens to that partner's ownership interest?
choice_a: It passes to the deceased partner's heirs according to the will
choice_b: It escheats to the state
choice_c: It is divided equally between the surviving joint tenant and the deceased partner's estate
choice_d: It passes automatically to the surviving joint tenant, regardless of what the deceased partner's will states
explanation: The defining feature of joint tenancy with right of survivorship is that a deceased joint tenant's interest passes automatically to the surviving joint tenant(s) by operation of law, bypassing probate and overriding any conflicting will provision.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A married couple takes title to their home in a form of ownership available only to married persons, which includes a right of survivorship and protects the property from the individual debts of only one spouse. This is:
choice_a: Tenancy by the entirety
choice_b: Tenancy in common
choice_c: Severalty
choice_d: A cooperative interest
explanation: Tenancy by the entirety is reserved for married couples, includes an automatic right of survivorship, and generally shields the property from a judgment against only one spouse individually, since neither spouse can convey or encumber the whole without the other's consent.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A grantor conveys property 'to my nephew for the life of my sister,' with the remainder to a charity. The nephew's interest is best described as a:
choice_a: Fee simple absolute
choice_b: Life estate pur autre vie, measured by the life of a person other than the life tenant himself
choice_c: Reversion
choice_d: Leasehold estate
explanation: A life estate pur autre vie is measured by the life of someone other than the life tenant -- here, the nephew holds the estate only for as long as his sister remains alive, after which the property passes to the named remainderman (the charity).
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A grantor conveys a life estate to her elderly aunt, with the deed stating that upon the aunt's death, title will revert back to the grantor. The grantor's future interest in this scenario is called a:
choice_a: Remainder
choice_b: Leasehold estate
choice_c: Reversion
choice_d: Easement in gross
explanation: When the future interest following a life estate goes back to the original grantor (or the grantor's heirs) rather than to a third party, it is called a reversion. If it instead passes to a named third party, it is called a remainder.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A buyer purchases a residential condominium unit. In addition to fee simple ownership of the interior airspace of the unit, what interest does the buyer typically also acquire?
choice_a: Shares in a corporation that owns the entire building
choice_b: A proprietary lease to occupy the unit
choice_c: A leasehold interest in the unit only, with no ownership interest at all
choice_d: An undivided tenancy-in-common interest in the building's common elements, such as the lobby, roof, and grounds
explanation: Condominium ownership combines fee simple title to the individual unit with an undivided tenancy-in-common interest, shared with all other unit owners, in the building's common elements and land.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A buyer purchases an apartment in a building where he receives shares of stock in the corporation that owns the entire building, along with a proprietary lease giving him the right to occupy a specific unit. This describes:
choice_a: Cooperative ownership
choice_b: Condominium ownership
choice_c: A timeshare interest
choice_d: Ownership in severalty
explanation: In a cooperative, a corporation holds title to the entire building, and residents own shares of the corporation rather than real property directly, with a proprietary lease granting the right to occupy a specific unit.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A buyer purchases the right to use a beachfront condo unit for one specific week every year, without owning the unit outright for the rest of the year. This is best described as:
choice_a: A life estate
choice_b: A timeshare (interval ownership or right-to-use arrangement)
choice_c: Tenancy by the entirety
choice_d: A leasehold estate for a term of one year
explanation: A timeshare divides the use of a property into fixed time intervals among multiple owners or users. It can be structured as fee interval ownership (a deeded fractional fee interest) or as a right-to-use arrangement (a contractual, non-ownership license for recurring use).
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: An individual buys a vacation home and takes title in her name alone, with no co-owners of any kind. This form of ownership is known as:
choice_a: Tenancy in common
choice_b: Joint tenancy
choice_c: Ownership in severalty
choice_d: Tenancy by the entirety
explanation: Ownership in severalty means title is held by a single person or single legal entity, with no co-owners -- the term comes from the owner's interest being 'severed' or separate from any other party.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership

question: A property owner transfers legal title to a piece of real estate to a trustee, who manages the property for the benefit of a named beneficiary who holds equitable title. This arrangement is known as:
choice_a: A life estate
choice_b: A leasehold estate
choice_c: Tenancy in common
choice_d: A trust, in which the trustee holds legal title while the beneficiary holds equitable (beneficial) title
explanation: In a real estate trust, the grantor (settlor) conveys legal title to a trustee, who has a fiduciary duty to manage the property for the benefit of the beneficiary, who holds equitable title and the beneficial enjoyment of the property.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership (broker-level: property held in trust)

question: A real estate investor uses a land trust to take title to an investment property, naming herself as beneficiary but appointing a trustee to hold recorded legal title. From a brokerage standpoint, one common reason investors use this structure is to:
choice_a: Keep the beneficial owner's identity out of the public land records, since the trustee's name appears on the recorded deed
choice_b: Avoid ever paying property taxes on the parcel
choice_c: Automatically convert the property into a condominium form of ownership
choice_d: Eliminate the need for title insurance at closing
explanation: A land trust allows a trustee to hold recorded legal title while the actual beneficiary's identity remains private, since only the trustee's name appears in the public record; brokers handling trust-held property must still verify who holds authority to sign on the trust's behalf.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership (broker-level: property held in trust)

question: A stranger has openly, continuously, and without the owner's permission occupied and used a strip of a neighbor's vacant land for the full statutory period required by state law, treating it as her own. Under the doctrine of adverse possession, what may result?
choice_a: The occupier automatically becomes a tenant of the true owner and owes back rent for the years of use
choice_b: The occupier may be able to acquire legal title to the strip of land, provided her possession was open, notorious, hostile, exclusive, and continuous for the statutory period
choice_c: The true owner retains title but must pay the occupier the value of any improvements made to the strip
choice_d: The occupier receives only a revocable license, never any claim to title
explanation: Adverse possession allows a non-owner who possesses land openly, notoriously, exclusively, continuously, and hostilely (without the true owner's permission) for the full statutory period to potentially obtain legal title to that land, typically by filing a quiet title action.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership (potential encumbrances: adverse possession)

question: A property is sold while a tenant is still occupying it under a valid, recorded lease with two years remaining. Unless the lease specifically terminates upon sale, what is generally true of the buyer's position?
choice_a: The sale automatically voids the lease and the tenant must vacate immediately
choice_b: The buyer may unilaterally raise the rent to market rate as soon as closing occurs
choice_c: The buyer takes title subject to the existing lease and must honor its terms until the lease expires
choice_d: The lease automatically converts into a month-to-month tenancy the moment the property changes hands
explanation: An existing lease is an encumbrance that runs with the land; a new owner generally takes title subject to the tenant's rights under the existing lease and must honor its terms for the remainder of its stated period.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership (potential encumbrances: existing leases)

question: A homeowner dies without having conveyed his property during his lifetime, so the property becomes part of his estate pending administration in probate court. Before the estate's personal representative may convey clear title to a buyer, what is generally required?
choice_a: Nothing at all; the property automatically becomes freely transferable the moment the owner dies
choice_b: The property must first be converted into a life estate before any sale can occur
choice_c: Title automatically vests in the county government until a buyer is located
choice_d: Probate court approval or documented authority confirming the personal representative's power to sell, since the decedent's estate itself now holds title
explanation: When an owner dies, title to real property held by the estate is subject to probate administration; a personal representative (executor or administrator) generally needs court-confirmed authority before conveying clear, marketable title to a buyer.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership (potential encumbrances/estate ownership: property in probate)

question: A subdivision's recorded declaration limits homes to single-family use and prohibits fences taller than four feet, binding all current and future lot owners in the development. This type of private land-use control is known as:
choice_a: A deed restriction (restrictive covenant), typically recorded in a declaration of covenants, conditions, and restrictions (CC&Rs)
choice_b: A public zoning ordinance enacted by the local municipality
choice_c: An easement in gross benefiting the original developer personally
choice_d: A license that expires once the developer sells the final lot
explanation: Deed restrictions, commonly recorded as CC&Rs, are private, contractual limitations on land use created by a developer or property owners' association that run with the land and bind future owners, unlike public zoning, which is government-imposed.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership (encumbrances: deed restrictions)

question: A recorded judgment against a debtor attaches to every parcel of real property that debtor owns within the recording county, rather than to one specific property. This type of lien is classified as a:
choice_a: Specific lien, which attaches only to one designated parcel
choice_b: General lien, which attaches to all of a debtor's property rather than to one specific parcel
choice_c: Easement, which grants a right of use rather than a security interest
choice_d: License, which is personal and non-transferable
explanation: A general lien, such as a recorded judgment lien, attaches to all real (and sometimes personal) property owned by the debtor in the jurisdiction, in contrast to a specific lien like a mortgage, which attaches to only one identified parcel.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership (liens and effect on title)

question: A homeowner willingly signs a mortgage to finance her home purchase. In contrast to a mechanic's lien filed without the owner's consent after a contractor goes unpaid, the mortgage is best classified as a:
choice_a: Involuntary lien, imposed on the property without the owner's consent
choice_b: General lien attaching to all of the owner's assets nationwide
choice_c: Voluntary lien, created intentionally through the property owner's own action
choice_d: Equitable lien arising solely from a court's sense of fairness
explanation: A mortgage is a voluntary lien because the owner knowingly and intentionally creates it to secure a loan, whereas liens like mechanic's liens, tax liens, and judgment liens are involuntary because they attach without the owner's consent.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership (liens: voluntary vs. involuntary)

question: A contractor completes renovation work on a home but is never paid. To secure payment, the contractor records a statutory claim against that specific property, even though the homeowner never signed any document creating the claim. This is an example of a:
choice_a: Easement by prescription acquired through the contractor's work on the property
choice_b: General lien covering all of the homeowner's other assets nationwide
choice_c: License, revocable by the homeowner at any time
choice_d: Mechanic's lien, a specific, involuntary lien available to unpaid contractors, subcontractors, and material suppliers who improve real property
explanation: A mechanic's lien is a specific, involuntary lien that unpaid contractors, subcontractors, and suppliers may file against the particular property they improved in order to secure payment for their labor or materials.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership (liens: mechanic's lien)

question: A property is subject to both a mortgage recorded in 2015 and unpaid current-year real estate property taxes. In a foreclosure sale, how are these two claims generally ranked against each other?
choice_a: The property tax lien has priority over the mortgage regardless of recording date, because tax liens generally hold superior ("superpriority") status
choice_b: The mortgage always has priority simply because it was recorded first in time
choice_c: The two liens must always be paid on a strictly equal, pro-rata basis
choice_d: Whichever lienholder files suit first automatically receives full priority over the other
explanation: Real estate property tax liens are generally given superpriority status, meaning they are paid ahead of other liens such as mortgages regardless of which was recorded first, reflecting the government's strong interest in collecting property taxes.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership (liens: priority)

question: A plaintiff files a lawsuit affecting title to a specific parcel and records a formal notice in the county land records warning potential buyers that the property's title is in dispute pending the outcome of litigation. This recorded notice is called:
choice_a: A deed of trust securing repayment of a loan
choice_b: A lis pendens ("suit pending"), which clouds title until the litigation is resolved
choice_c: A quitclaim deed releasing any interest in the property
choice_d: An estoppel certificate confirming lease terms
explanation: A lis pendens is a recorded notice that litigation affecting title to a specific property is pending; it clouds the title and warns prospective buyers or lenders of the dispute until the lawsuit is resolved.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership (potential encumbrances: pending litigation)

question: A parcel becomes completely landlocked after its owner sells off the only strip of land that provided access to the public road. Even though no written agreement was ever made, a court may grant the landlocked owner a right to cross the seller's remaining land. This is an example of:
choice_a: An easement by prescription, based on adverse use over a statutory period of time
choice_b: A license, which the servient landowner may revoke at will
choice_c: An easement by necessity, implied by law to provide access to an otherwise landlocked parcel
choice_d: An easement in gross benefiting the original seller personally
explanation: An easement by necessity arises by operation of law, without any written agreement, when a parcel is landlocked as a result of a conveyance, ensuring the landlocked owner has legally enforceable access across the remaining land.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership (easements: by necessity)

question: For twenty consecutive years, a neighbor has openly and continuously driven across a corner of an adjoining owner's land without permission, and state law recognizes an eighteen-year prescriptive period. What has the neighbor most likely acquired?
choice_a: Fee simple title to the corner of land by adverse possession, since a right of use requires the same exclusivity as title
choice_b: A license, which the landowner may still revoke at any time
choice_c: No rights at all, because an easement can only be created by a written, recorded agreement
choice_d: An easement by prescription, arising from open, notorious, continuous, and hostile use of another's land for the statutory period
explanation: An easement by prescription is acquired through open, notorious, continuous, and hostile use of another's land for the statutory period; unlike adverse possession, it grants only a right of use, not title, and typically does not require exclusive use.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership (easements: by prescription)

question: Two attached townhomes share a single wall that sits exactly on the boundary line between the two lots, with each owner entitled to use the wall and obligated to help maintain it. This shared structure is known as a:
choice_a: Party wall, subject to a party wall easement shared by both adjoining owners
choice_b: Trade fixture belonging solely to one of the two owners
choice_c: Riparian boundary marker
choice_d: License, revocable by either owner at will
explanation: A party wall straddles the boundary line between two adjoining properties, and each owner holds an easement (a party wall easement) to use and a shared duty to help maintain the common structure.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership (easements: party wall)

question: A survey ordered before closing reveals that the seller's garage roof overhangs onto the neighboring lot by two feet. If this encroachment is not resolved before closing, what is the most likely effect on the transaction?
choice_a: It has no effect on the transaction because encroachments are automatically cured at closing by operation of law
choice_b: It may render title unmarketable, since the buyer could face a legal claim from the neighboring owner over the encroaching structure
choice_c: It automatically transfers ownership of the encroaching portion of the garage to the neighboring owner
choice_d: It automatically converts the encroachment into a valid easement by necessity
explanation: An unresolved encroachment can cloud title and render it unmarketable, since the neighboring owner could bring a legal claim (such as for trespass or removal) against the encroaching structure after closing.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership (encroachments: effect on title)

question: A riparian landowner's property gradually gains additional land over many years as soil is deposited along the riverbank by the natural action of the flowing water. This gradual, natural increase in land is called:
choice_a: Avulsion, a sudden loss of land caused by a natural force
choice_b: Escheat, a transfer of property to the state
choice_c: Accretion, which gives the riparian owner title to the newly deposited land
choice_d: Eminent domain, a government taking of private property
explanation: Accretion is the gradual, natural buildup of soil or land along a waterway caused by the action of water; the riparian or littoral owner generally acquires title to the newly accreted land.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership (water rights: accretion)

question: A sudden flood dramatically and instantly shifts a river's channel overnight, cutting off a portion of a riparian owner's land. Under the doctrine of avulsion, what generally happens to the original property boundary?
choice_a: The boundary automatically shifts to follow the river's new channel, exactly as it would under accretion
choice_b: The owner immediately and permanently loses all riparian rights to any water
choice_c: Title to the cut-off land automatically escheats to the state
choice_d: The original boundary line generally remains fixed at its former location despite the sudden change in the river's course
explanation: Avulsion is a sudden, perceptible change in a waterway's course caused by a natural event such as a flood. Unlike accretion, avulsion does not shift the legal boundary, which generally remains at its pre-avulsion location.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership (water rights: avulsion)

question: In the government (rectangular) survey system, the primary vertical and horizontal reference lines from which township and range measurements are made are called, respectively:
choice_a: The principal meridian, running north-south, and the base line, running east-west
choice_b: The lot line and the block line
choice_c: The metes line and the bounds line
choice_d: The section line and the quarter-section line
explanation: The government survey system is built around a principal meridian (a north-south reference line) and a base line (an east-west reference line), from which townships are measured in tiers and ranges.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership (government survey: reference lines)

question: Within a single township under the government survey system, the 36 sections are numbered in a serpentine (boustrophedon) pattern. Where is Section 1 located, and how does the numbering proceed?
choice_a: Section 1 is always located in the exact center of the township
choice_b: Section 1 is in the northeast corner of the township, and numbering proceeds west across the top row, then snakes back east along the next row down, continuing in that back-and-forth pattern
choice_c: Section 1 is in the southwest corner, and numbering proceeds directly north in straight columns
choice_d: Sections are numbered in a different, non-standardized order in every state
explanation: Sections within a township are numbered 1 through 36 in a standardized serpentine pattern beginning with Section 1 in the northeast corner, moving west across the top tier, then reversing direction on each successive row down to Section 36 in the southeast corner.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership (government survey: section numbering)

question: A parcel is legally described as the Northeast quarter of the Southwest quarter of a section. How many acres does this parcel contain?
choice_a: 160 acres
choice_b: 10 acres
choice_c: 40 acres
choice_d: 80 acres
explanation: A full section contains 640 acres. A quarter of a quarter section is calculated as 640 divided by 4, divided by 4 again, which equals 40 acres.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership (government survey: acreage calculation)

question: Courts apply several tests to decide whether an item has become a fixture. Which test is generally considered the most important, since it can override other factors such as the method of physical attachment?
choice_a: The item's original purchase price
choice_b: The number of years the item has remained on the property
choice_c: Whether the item happens to be mentioned by brand name in the listing
choice_d: The intention of the party who installed or attached the item at the time of installation
explanation: While courts weigh multiple fixture tests, the intention of the party who installed the item is generally regarded as the most important, since it can outweigh factors like method of attachment when determining whether an item was meant to become part of the real property.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership (fixtures: intention test)

question: Fixture disputes are resolved differently depending on who is disputing the item. Between a seller and a buyer, courts tend to presume an attached item is a fixture and favor the buyer; between a landlord and a commercial tenant, courts instead tend to favor the tenant's right to remove trade fixtures. This variation in outcome illustrates which fixture test?
choice_a: The relationship-of-the-parties test
choice_b: The adaptability-to-use test
choice_c: The method-of-attachment test
choice_d: A rule requiring a written fixture agreement in every transaction
explanation: The relationship-of-the-parties test recognizes that courts favor different outcomes depending on who is disputing an item's status -- generally favoring buyers over sellers, and favoring tenants' rights to remove trade fixtures over landlords.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership (fixtures: relationship of parties test)

question: A manufactured home is permanently placed on a poured concrete foundation, has its wheels and axles removed, and is connected to permanent utility lines on land the homeowner also owns. Under general property law, this manufactured home most likely becomes classified as:
choice_a: Personal property indefinitely, because manufactured homes can never legally become real property under any circumstances
choice_b: Real property, because it has been permanently affixed to the land in a manner that satisfies the general fixture tests
choice_c: A trade fixture, removable by the homeowner at any time
choice_d: An emblement, harvested annually like a crop
explanation: A manufactured home that is permanently affixed to land the owner also owns -- with wheels and axles removed and a permanent foundation and utility connections -- generally satisfies the fixture tests and converts from personal property (a vehicle/chattel) into real property.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership (fixtures: manufactured housing)

question: A limited liability company (LLC) purchases an office building and takes title in the LLC's own name as the sole owner of record, even though the LLC itself has several individual members. This form of holding title is best classified as:
choice_a: Tenancy in common among the LLC's individual members
choice_b: Joint tenancy among the LLC's individual members
choice_c: Ownership in severalty by a business entity, since the LLC alone is the titleholder even though it has multiple members
choice_d: A cooperative form of ownership
explanation: A single business entity, such as a corporation, LLC, or partnership, can hold title alone -- this is still ownership in severalty, since only one legal person (the entity itself) is the titleholder, regardless of how many individual members or shareholders make up that entity.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership (types of ownership: business entity ownership)

question: Real property ownership is often described as a "bundle of legal rights" rather than ownership of the physical land itself. Which of the following best reflects this concept?
choice_a: Ownership is a single, indivisible right that can never be separated into component parts
choice_b: The bundle of rights concept applies only to personal property and never to real property
choice_c: The bundle of rights consists exclusively of the right to sell the property
choice_d: Ownership includes separate rights such as the right to possess, use, transfer, encumber, and exclude others, any of which can be conveyed or retained separately from the rest
explanation: The bundle of legal rights concept describes real property ownership as a collection of distinct rights -- to possess, use, transfer, encumber, and exclude others -- each of which the owner can retain, convey, or separately transfer, as seen with easements, leases, and mineral rights.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Property Ownership (bundle of rights)
